#### Summary

A large state of the art circle and text based image classification methods relied on color- and time-based factors. To expand the number and breadth of approaches, we study a new way: circle detection and drawing algorithms, based on image processing and graphics design. Soon after, most circle detection and drawing algorithms were realized with a wide range of circumferences and time-horizon scales. To evaluate circles for non-cartographic regions, translation and rotation are not required. Almost all the previously mentioned algorithms achieved quite good classification database results, but they could not consider all possible transformations of the circle around its center by rotation.

Next, we proposed two new circle algorithms for untransformed images and manually created ones and added circle contours with image, circle and text content. They achieved good classification results. To evaluate non-fully automated approaches, we also proposed SiamCRRNN, an adapted []RCNN, with parts of sliding windows derived from the popular CXG method to eliminate most of the drawbacks.

The first variational algorithm, incorporating the MF assumption and integrating PF for latent state inference, was introduced in [25]. Subsequent MF endeavors [26]–[28] aimed at reducing computational and model complexities in [25].While the MF class methods may enable more manageable computations, they neglect the inherent dependencies between the latent states and the GP dynamics, potentially impairing the overall learning accuracy and yielding overconfident state estimates [35].

Represent methods [29]–[33], therefore, concentrate on the more complicated NMF approximation to address the inac-curacies arising from the MF assumption, yet they continue to struggle with computational challenges. Specifically, in [29],the posterior distribution of underlying states conditioned on the GP dynamics was simply approximated by the subjectively selected prior distribution, while in [30] and [31], the poste-rior was approximated by some parametric Markov-structured Gaussian variational distributions. However, optimizing the extensive variational parameters in the variational distributions is computationally demanding and inefficient. In contrast to the heavy parameterization as conducted in [29]–[31], the works in [32] and [33] opted for directly characterizing the pos-terior distribution through the model evidence. Nonetheless,the the Laplace approximation, employed in [32], can yield an oversimplified unimodal posterior distribution over the latentstates [17], while the stochastic gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo method [36], employed in [33], may exhibit very slow convergence (50,000 iterations as reported). Furthermore,all these existing variational methods are incompatible with online applications, posing a notable limitation in their applicability.

To tackle the computational challenges mentioned above,we propose integrating the model-based filtering technique,EnKF, into the NMF variational inference framework. The primary benefit of this approach lies in the streamlineProvide a guide to utmost importance. parameterization of the associated variational distributions,improving inference tractability and accelerating algorithm convergence. Additionally, this streamline characterization enables seamless accommodation of our method in online learningapplications. The main contributions are summarized as follows.

We corroborate the significance of incorporating well-established model-based filtering techniques to enhance the efficiency of GPSSM variational algorithms. In contrast to existing methods utilizing numerous variational parameters to parameterize the variational distribution over latent states,our proposed novel algorithm harnesses the EnKF to accurately capture the dependencies between the latent states and the GP dynamics, and eliminate the need to parameterize the variational distribution, significantly reducing the number of variational parameters and accelerating the algorithm convergence.

Remark 1. _It is important to note the distinction between GPSSMs and the state-space representation of GPs (SSGP). The SSGP is a method that converts a GP into a linear state-space form, enabling the use of efficient inference techniques such as the Kalman filter and smoother, thereby facilitating the computationally efficient handling of large-scale problems. For more details on SSGP, we direct readers to [40], [41]. In contrast, a GPSSM utilizes the non-parametric flexibility of GPs to model the state transitions in SSMs, allowing for the capture of complex, nonlinear system dynamics. This results in a more flexible but typically computationally intensive SSM._

Given the aforementioned model, see Eq. (5), the joint density function of the GPSSM can be expressed as:

\[ p(\vec{\mathbf{f}},\vec{\mathbf{x}},\vec{\mathbf{y}}|{\mathbf{\theta}})= p(\mathbf{x}_{0})p(\mathbf{f}_{1:T})\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(\mathbf{y}_{t}|\mathbf{x} _{t})p(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\mathbf{f}_{t}),\] (6)

 where \(p(\mathbf{f}_{1:T})\)=\(p(f(\mathbf{x}_{0:T-1})\))=\(\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(\mathbf{f}_{t}|\mathbf{f}_{1:t-1},\mathbf{x}_{0:t-1})\) correspond to a finite dimensional (\(T\)-dimensional) GP distribution [26], and we define the short-hand notations \(\vec{\mathbf{y}}\triangleq\mathbf{y}_{1:T}={\{\mathbf{y}_{t}\}}_{t=1}^{T}\), \(\vec{\mathbf{f}}\triangleq\mathbf{f}_{1:T}=\{\mathbf{f}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}\), and \(\vec{\mathbf{x}}\triangleq\mathbf{x}_{0:T}=\{\mathbf{x}_{t}\}_{t=0}^{T}\). The model parameters \(\mathbf{\theta}\) includes the noise covariance and GP hyper-parameters, i.e., \(\mathbf{\theta}\)={\(Q,\mathbf{R},\mathbf{\theta}_{gp}\)}. The challenging task in GPSSM is to learn \(\mathbf{\theta}\), and simultaneously infer the latent states of interest, which involves the marginal distribution \(p(\vec{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{\theta})\). However, due to the nonlinearity of GP, a closed-form solution for \(p(\vec{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{\theta})\) is unavailable. Hence, it becomes necessary to utilize approximation methods.

III. PROBLEM STATEMENT

To overcome the intractability of the marginal distribution \(p(\vec{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{\theta})\), variational GPSSMs involve constructing a model evidence lower bound (ELBO) to the logarithm of the marginal likelihood. Specifically, the ELBO, denoted by \(\mathcal{L}\), is constructed such that the difference between \(\log p(\vec{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{\theta})\) and \(\mathcal{L}\) is equal to the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the variational approximation, \(q(\vec{\mathbf{x}},\vec{\mathbf{f}})\), and the true posterior, \(p(\vec{\mathbf{x}},\vec{\mathbf{f}}|\vec{\mathbf{y}})\), i.e.,

\[\log p(\vec{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{\theta})-\mathbb{E}_{q(\vec{\mathbf{x}},\vec{ \mathbf{f}})}\bigg{[}\underbrace{\log\frac{p(\vec{\mathbf{f}},\vec{\mathbf{x}} ,\vec{\mathbf{y}})}{q(\vec{\mathbf{x}},\vec{\mathbf{f}})}}_{\Delta\mathcal{L}}=\underbrace{KL\bigg{[}q(\vec{\mathbf{x}},\vec{\mathbf{f}})||p(\vec{\mathbf{x}},\vec{ \mathbf{f}}|\vec{\mathbf{y}})\cdot\bigg{]}_{\geq 0}}_{\geq 0}\bigg{]}.\] (7)

 Detailed derivations a can be found in Supplement A-A. Maximizing \(\mathcal{L}\) with respect to (w.r.t.) \(\mathbf{\theta}\) fine-tunes the model

### (d) Video Processing

Fig. 5 illustrates the divide-frame algorithm in terms of video processing. The algorithm aims to detect flow patterns and extract salient regions at various scales. Initially, the algorithm estimates paths for a stack of frames by tracking or structuring as the algorithm traverses through the video stream at a frame rate. The algorithms evaluate whether paths meet high-end criterions such as specific interest points, video structures, and image-text pairs. The interest points are detected by maximizing \( Q(\vec{x},\vec{F})/D \). This function rejects very low probability paths and attempts to highlight著名 near-fallible decoding parameters via local regression. For all experimental videos, the interest points often exhibit pedestrian or object-wise projections.

To address these limitations, we step away from the heavy parameterization (e.g., the black-box inference networks) and propose a novel interpretable EnKF-aided algorithm for variational inference in GpSSMs. Our algorithm can exploit the dependencies between \(\vec{x}~\) and \(\vec{F} \), and alleviate the mode and computational complexities while being easily extended to an online learning algorithm.

### IV. ENVI: ENKF-AIDED VARIATIONAL INFERENCE

This section presents our novel variational inference algorithm for GPSSMs. We begin by introducing the model-based EnKF in Section IV-A, which serves as the foundation for our algorithm. Following that, Section IV-B details the proposed EnKF-aided variational inference algorithm. Lastly, extensive discussions about the properties of our proposed algorithm are given in Section IV-C.

#### A. Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF)

The EnKF is a Monte Carlo-based method that excels in handling nonlinear systems compared to the KF and EKF [45]. Given an SSM, see Eq. (4), the EnKF sequentially approximates the filtering distributions using \(e\N e ofinMM\) equally weighted particles [45]. Specifically, at the prediction step, EnKF first samples particles, \(x_{ t-1}^{t=N}\subset\{x_{ 1-1}^{n} \}^{N}_{n=1}\), from the filtering distribution, \(p(x_{ t-1} | y_{1:t-1})\), at time \(t-1\). Then, the sampled particles are propagated using the state transition function \(f(\cdot)\), i.e.,

\[\vec{x}^{n}_{t} = f(x_{ t-1}^{n}) + \mathbf{v}^{n}_{t}, \mathbf{v}^{n}_{t} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, Q),\ \forall n.\] (10)

The prediction distribution is then approximated by a Gaussian distribution, i.e. \(p(x_{ t}|y_{1:t-1}) \sim \mathcal{N}(x_{t}|\bar{m}_{t},\bar{P}_{t})\), where

\[\bar{m}_{t} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \vec{x}^{n}_{t},\] (11a) \[\bar{P}_{t} = \frac{1}{N-1} \sum_{n=1}^{N} (\vec{x}^{n}_{t}- \bar{m}_{t})(\vec{x}^{n}_{t}- \bar{m}_{t})^{\top}.\] (11b)

With the linear Gaussian emission in Eq. (4), the joint distribution of \( x_{t} \) and \( y_{ t} \) can be readily obtained as follows:

\[\begin{bmatrix} x_{t}|y_{1:t- 1} \\ y_{ t}|y_{ 1:t- 1} \end{bmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N} \left ( \begin{bmatrix} \bar{m}_{ t}\\ C\bar{m}_{ t}\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} \bar{P}_{ t}, & \bar{P}_{ t}C^{\top} \\ C\bar{P}_{ t}, & C\bar{P}_{ t}C^{\top} + R\end{bmatrix} \right).\] (12)

Thus, the filtering distribution, \( p(x_{ t}| y_{1:t}) = \mathcal{N}(x_{ t}|\bar{m}_{t},\bar{P}_{t})\), can be obtained using the conditional Gaussian identity at the update step, where

\[\mathbf{m}_{t} = \bar{m}_{t} + \bar{G}_{t}(y_{ t} - C \bar{m} _{t}),\] (13a) \[\mathbf{P}_{ t} = \bar{P}_{ t} - \bar{P}_{ t}C^{\top}\bar{G}^{\top}_{t},\] (13b)

and \(\bar{G}_{t} = \bar{P}_{ t}C^{\top}(C \bar{P}_{ t}C^{\top} + R)^{-1}\) is the Kalman gain [45]. Each filtered particle \( x^{n}_{ t}\) is then obtained from a Kalman-type update, i.e.,

\[x^{n}_{t} = \bar{x}^{n}_{t} + \bar{G}_{t}(y_{ t} + \mathbf{e}_{t}^{n} - C\bar{x}^{n}_{t}), \mathbf{e}_{t}^{n} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, R),\ \ \forall n.\] (14)

It is crucial to note that the EnKF inherently exhibits differentiability. Specifically, if we utilize the reparameterization trick [46] to sample the process and observation noises as shown in Eq. (10) and (14), i.e.,

\[\mathbf{v}^{n}_{t} = 0 + Q_{2}^{\frac{1}{2}}\bm{\epsilon}, \bm{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{I}_{d_{ x}}),\] (15a) \[\mathbf{e}_{ t}^{n} = 0 + \mathbf {R}^{\frac{1}{2}}\bm{\epsilon}, \bm{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{I}_{ d_{ y}}),\] (15b)

**3.4 Ledbetter’s chaotic encryption system for the proposed methods**

If in the Ledbetter’s chaotic encryption system, set a large a finite number \(T\), the PDE system (7)-(9) can be transformed into the following _Allton-Rudin-Segur Barker (ARS) equation_\[ \begin{cases} y(k) = ps(x) + F(y(k-1,z)) + J(x(k,z)), \ k \in [1,T] \\ y(k+T) = y(k) + J(x(k,z))+D(x(k)) \end{cases} \]\(z=0,1,...,P\) in the ARS equation, \(F\) is the step function \(\begin{cases} ps(z) = a(L^B(z))[q(z)]_T & \text{if } z \leq L^B, \\ ps(z) = a(L^B(z))[q(z)]_T + b^B(z)[g(z)]_T & \text{if } z > L^B \end{cases}\), Quaternary adaptive channel model\[ F(\mathbf{y}) = [A_{d}^{(1)} \ \cdots \ A_{d}^{(T)}]Q, \] where \(A_{d}^{(i)} \in C^{1 \times P}\) are coefficients between Husimi parameter set and the query generator, \(Q \in C^T\) is the decoder input for QR \(B\) pulse. In this paper, we use HDMI as a RSEP link and the conditional distribution of a binary rope model of ARS equation is given by

  **3.5 ARS security equation**

In Ledbetter’s chaotic encryption system, copyright was strengthened in order to defeat copying, provoking a rich family of multimedia encryption approaches. In the ARS equation [17], the copyright is established by the worst noise, which means that the chaotic signal is an essential characteristic of the system and the trusted encryption, rather than an initial condition scalar. Besides the original design previously proposed [17], Ledbetter’s chaotic encryption system has been improved for the following reasons: 1) The derivation is by searching the chaotic mappings between noiseless properties and auditor’s privacy requirements, 2) The chaotic sequence is not recorded distance, and other features including mathematical transformation of the encrypted matrix, key length.

The following equivalent undecoded encrypted signal can be computed as

\[ {Q} = [Ss.][A_{d}^{(1)} \ \cdots \ A_{d}^{(T)}][Ys.][A_{d}^{(1)} \ \cdots \ A_{d}^{(T)}]Q \]

where \([A_{d}^{(i)}]_{P \times P}\) is the digital noise inverse matrix. The secrecy enhancement is realized by the MULTICHANNEL mar457]{A} function of ARS equation, which is a complement program for the proposal of Ledbetter’s chaotic encryption a high secure encryption method.

**3. 4 Self-supervised plaintext data generation and extraction**

The self-supervised plaintext generation process is shown in figure 6. A MQS model is first trained to perform cross-domain prediction for a given plaintext \(\mathbf{x}\) by incorporating additional models, for instance, a cycle classifier network. Secondly, reference plaintexts \(\textbf{x_{ref}}^T\) with \(\mathbf{x}\) are fed into the prediction model for prediction will generate cross-domain prediction results. Using cross-domain prediction results for cross-domain rejection processing, the proposed model becomes more accurate.

**3.Synthesis of the proposed model**

According to Lemma 1, and the ELBO given in Eq. (37), we immediately get the following approximated ELBO:

\[\mathcal{L}\approx\mathbb{E}_{q(\bar{\textbf{u}})}\Bigg{[} \sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p(\mathbf{y}_{t}|\bar{\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{y}_ {1:t-1})\Bigg{]}\ - \mathrm{KL}[q(\mathbf{x}_{0})||p(\mathbf{x}_{0})]\ \ \ \ (40)\] (44) \[-\mathrm{ KL}[q(\bar{\mathbf{u}})||p(\bar{\mathbf{u}})],\]

where the log-likelihood, \(\log p(\mathbf{y}_{t}|\bar{\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{y}_{1:t-1})\) in Eq. (40) can be analytically evaluated using EnKF, see Eq. (27), due to the Gaussian prediction distribution, see Eq. (25), and the linear emission model.

**Appendix B** **PROOF OF PROPOSITION 2** _Preof._ With the filtering distribution\( p(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\bar{\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{y}_{1:t})\) ,we have the log-likelihood term \[\log p(\mathbf{y}_{t}|\bar{\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{y}_{1:t-1})\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ (42a)\] \[= \mathbb{E}_{p(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\bar{\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{y}_{1:t})} \left[\log p(\mathbf{y}_{t}|\bar{\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{y}_{1:t-1})\right] \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ (42b)\] \[= \mathbb{E}_{p(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\bar{\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{y}_{1:t})} \left[\log\frac{p(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\bar{\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{y}_{1:t-1})p(\mathbf {y}_{t}|\mathbf{x}_{t})}{p(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\bar{\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{y}_{1:t-1}, \mathbf{y}_{t})}\right] \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ (42c)\] \[= -\mathbb{E}_{p(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\bar{\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{y}_{1:t})} \left[\log\frac{p(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\bar{\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{y}_{1:t})}{p(\mathbf {x}_{t}|\bar{\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{y}_{1:t-1})p(\mathbf{y}_{t}|\mathbf{x}_{t})} \right] \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ (42d)\] \[= -\mathrm{ KL}\left[p(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\bar{\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{y}_{1:t-1}) ||p(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\bar{\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{y}_{1:t-1})\right]\] \[+\mathbb{E}_{p(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\bar{\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{y}_{1:t})} \left[\log p(\mathbf{y}_{t}|\mathbf{x}_{t})\right], (42e)\]

which completes the proof. Here Eq. (42c) is obtained straightforwardly by applying Bayes’ theorem. This result sheds light on the interplay between data reconstruction and the alignment of filtering and prediction distributions in the EnVI and OENVI algorithms.\(\square\)

**Appendix C**

**MEAN-FIELD AND NON-MEAN-FIELD APPROXIMATIONS**

**Definition 1.**_If the variational distribution, \( q(\vec{\mathbf{f}},\vec{\mathbf{u}},\vec{\mathbf{x}})\),is factorized such that the transition function values and the latent states are independent, i.e.,_

\[ q(\vec{\mathbf{f}},\vec{\mathbf{u}})q(\mathbf{x}_{0})\prod_{t=1}^{T}q(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\vec{\mathbf{f}}_{t})=q(\vec{\mathbf{f}},\vec{\mathbf{u}})q(\vec{\mathbf{x}}), \]\]
  (43)

_the factorization is known as a mean-field approximation in the GPSSM literature. Conversely, if the variational distribution, \( q(\vec{\mathbf{x}},\vec{\mathbf{f}},\vec{\mathbf{u}})\), explicitly builds the dependence between the latent states and the transition function values, as shown in Eq. (8), it is a non-mean-field approximation. \boxed{\quad}\)

In Bayesian statistics, the model marginal likelihood \(p(\vec{y}|\theta)\) is a fundamental quantity for model selection and comparison [43]. By maximizing the logarithm of \(p(\vec{y}|\theta)\) w.r.t. the model parameters \(\theta\), the goodness of data fitting and the model complexity are automatically balanced, in accordance with Occam's razor principle [42]. However, \(p(\vec{y}|\theta)\) is obtained by integrating out all the latent variables \(\{\vec{x}, \vec{f}\}\) in the joint distribution, see Eq. (16), which is analytically intractable. Thus, the posterior distribution of the latent variables, \(p(\vec{x}, \vec{f}|\vec{y}) = \frac{p(\vec{y}, \vec{x}, \vec{f})}{p(\vec{y}|\theta)}\), cannot be expressed in a closed-form expression, either. This intractability issue has been addressed in variational Bayesian methods by adopting a variational distribution [17], \(q(\vec{x}, \vec{f})\), to approximate the intractable \(p(\vec{x}, \vec{f}|\vec{y})\). With the newly introduced variational distribution \(q(\vec{x}, \vec{f})\), we have

\[\log p(\vec{y}|\theta) = \log \frac{p(\vec{y}, \vec{x}, \vec{f})}{p(\vec{x}, \vec{f}|\vec{y})} = \int \int q(\vec{x}, \vec{f}) \log \frac{p(\vec{y}, \vec{x}, \vec{f}) q(\vec{x}, \vec{f})}{p(\vec{x}, \vec{f}|\vec{y}) q(\vec{x}, \vec{f})} d\vec{x} d\vec{f}\]

\[= \mathbb{E}_{q(\vec{x}, \vec{f})} \left[ \log \frac{p(\vec{y}, \vec{x}, \vec{f})}{q(\vec{x}, \vec{f})} \right] + \mathbb{E}_{q(\vec{x}, \vec{f})} \left[ \log \frac{q(\vec{x}, \vec{f})}{p(\vec{x}, \vec{f}|\vec{y})} \right]\]

(44)

\[= \mathbb{E}_{q(\vec{x}, \vec{f})} \left[ \sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{d=1}^{d_x} (\hat{x}^{(d)}_t - x^{(d)}_t)^2 \right]\]

(45)

The definition of RMSE:

\[\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{d=1}^{d_x} (\hat{x}^{(d)}_t - x^{(d)}_t)^2}\]

Where \(\hat{x}_t\) represents the estimation of \(\mathbf{x}_t\).

- The baseline in Table III and Table IV is the RMSE between the noisy observations \(\mathbf{y}_{1:T}\) and the latent states \(\mathbf{x}_{1:T}\).
- Table III, and Figs. 7 and 8 present the results obtained using our proposed methods, EnVI and OEnVI, applied to learning the linear Gaussian SSM with the identity coefficient matrix \(\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{I}_{4 \times 4}\).
- The results in Table IV and Fig. 6 show that our proposed methods, EnVI and OEnVI, can still accurately filter the true latent states. However, it is noteworthy that the matrix \(C \in \mathbb{R}^{d_y \times d_x}\) should be “full-column rank” if the main task is to perform filtering; otherwise, there is a high probability that some latent dimensions cannot be inferred accurately. Intuitively speaking, if we aim to recover latent state \(\mathbf{x}_t\), it is only possible when the corresponding observation \(\mathbf{y}_t\) contains “sufficient information” about \(\mathbf{x}_t\). For the task of predicting the sequence \(\mathbf{y}_t\) for \(t = T+1, T+2, \ldots\), it is typically not necessary to focus as much on the physical meaning and accuracy of the latent states.

\[
\text{Horizon metric} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \max_{t \leq s} P(s, i)
\]

where \(P\) is the policy (action) distribution for state \(s\) and for time \(t\), \(s \leq t\). The \(\max\) here denotes taking the maximum over all possible consecutive states beyond which the epoch ends (note that future states not contemplated for the maximum are not considered). When exactly one immediate discount factor \(\gamma_0 \in \Delta[0, 1]\) and that horizon metric is used for the max-margin part of the instance-freetour algorithm, i.e. when \(\lambda[0] \equiv 2^{-L}\) and \(L \approx \infty\) in (36), the switching-rate structure is irreducible: This implies loss of nonlinear dimensionality and hence a large number of decision variables in the case of a medium-sized Farey tree. The resulting algorithm is remarkable fast because of the large number of independent \(W_\xi\). When this is not the case and the horizon metric is used for part of the instance-freetours algorithm, i.e. when either \(\lambda[0] = 2^{-L} \) and \(L < \infty\), or \(\lambda[0] = 0\) (in which case \(\lambda_L[0] < 2^{-L}\)) and \(\lambda[0] < \infty\), the algorithm needs to select a tunable number \(L\) of levels in the Farey tree to predict the future state \(s \leq t\). An algorithm selecting \(L\) levels out of \(n\) choices has a fraction of relevant options of \((1-\lambda_L[0]|s=s, t)\) equal to \(\lambda_L[0]\), to which will yield nontrivial returns.

The algorithm of Example 1 can be better understood if written as a sequence of two decisions \(\xi_1\) and \(\xi_2\); while the action \(\xi_1\) is always 1 and is omitted from considerations. In other words, the algorithm of Example 1 becomes the deterministic variant of the two-stepping algorithm for deciding \(W_{\xi_2}\) from \(W_{\xi_1}\), which in rounds \(n\) yields:

[Theorem 2] Assuming that Model (21) is a correct underlying model of one-time-POI, for any \(\xi \in \Delta[0, 1]\) with \(\lambda[0] > 0\), using Formula 27 the normalized mean value for Equation (37) for epoch durations close to \(\frac{1}{2}/\lambda[0] + O(|\lambda[0] - \lambda_L|)^{-1}\), with \(\lambda(L) = \lambda[L]\) and therefore with \(W_{\xi_2}\) from \(W_{\xi_1}\) unscathed, approximates the optimal final discounted value of the instance-freetour algorithm up to \(O(|\lambda[0] - \lambda_L|)^{-1}\) to within a multiplicative error of an order \(|\lambda[0] - \lambda_L|\).

Due to the manner in which the algorithm exactly exploits in the Farey tree the periodicity of \(\lambda[0]\), the optimal initial action \(\xi_1\) is never active. It follows that \(W_{\xi_1}=1\) if \(\lambda[0] \geq 1\) and \(W_{\xi_1} = S/2\) if \(\lambda[0] < 1\). This means that the algorithm iterates overtime until the action starts to be relevant (non-deterministically) until one of the following events occurs: the horizon metric reaches its maximum above the utility of \(W_{\xi_1}\) (state in which the state \(s \leq t\) is not the best immediate guess for \(W_{\xi_1}\) hence the algorithm stops and greedily picks the next immediate guess for \(W_{\xi_1}\)), or a transition to state \(s \geq t\) occurs and then is stuck until time \(0\). For \(s \geq t\) the choice of the action \(\xi_2\) and the corresponding reward \(P_{s,t}[0] = 0\) is no longer relevant and is thus discarded.

The spin glass order parameter [36] (which we normalize so that it has a maximum value of \(1\) on the ordered state and a minimum of \(0\) on the disordered state) is plotted for different temperatures and various system sizes (experimentally estimated using the data from Fig. 8.) As happens with all systems exhibiting the same physical mechanisms, the mean-field predictions (gray lines) at each temperature agree quite well with the data (colored symbols) for all system sizes. A confidence coherence band, which is defined as the range within which 95% of the data lies, is given by the formula \(N_{0}\pm 4N_{10}^{-1/2}\). We observe that our results for \(N_{0}\) are 10 times smaller than predicted. This small difference can be explained by the fact that the mean-field theory uses a length and time constant for competing forces which are equal to each other (see Eq. (47)), without considering the effect of temperature on the competing force. The experimental results for each temperature might be better modeled with a length and time constant that might have several orders of magnitude larger values.

At small system sizes, for the models that include competing forces, \(N_{0}\) approaches zero for all three temperatures. This is to be expected (verification of expectation (47)) as the system quickly reaches a disordered uniform state at any local minima (verification of expectation (42)) and corresponding use of Hamiltonian expansion (verification of expectation (42)) of Boltzmann function is inapplicable (in the case \(T=0\)). Moreover, in Fig. 7, the variance of \(N_{0}\) initially shows some enhancement, which we think is intuitively plausible, as all excitations come from \(p=1\) vertices of which there are many, alternating with \(p=0\) vertices. Thus two or four excitations exist simultaneously contributing with each step to the effective energies pushing the system toward zero excitations. For the other models, which do not have competing forces, \(N_{0}\) converges to zero for small system sizes. No convincing theory to explain this behavior exists currently, and the red line in Fig. 7 could be a non-thermal glass transition in a model without competing forces, or an effect due to finite size [44, 45].

For medium system sizes, \(N_{0}\) increases with temperature, mainly due to the fact that the spins are warmer, and with the linear increase of the momentum distribution function, which also contributes to the competition between the two extreme orientations of the spin. As it rises, the system approaches to the fully ordered state, and in this critical region the information on the status of the spin is transferred efficiently to the degrees of freedom of the heat flow, thus the typical "railroad track" fluctuation diffuses parallel to the chosen direction of transport. Beyond a moment on the occurrence of a single spin glass transition, \(N_{0}\) begins to decrease as the spike integrated spin glass order parameter never hits zero at any local minima, and the plateau level remains physically appropriate for the system characterized quantitatively by \(\gamma=2\). For the model that includes competing forces, there tends to be a rapid temperature dependence of \(N_{0}\), and the plateau is shed with more heat supply, warming up the thermal glass transition to the system size criticality. The smallness of the plateau height is natural as the information takes time to be transferred and transmitted, and it is also legitimate due to the small values of the overall heat capacity (subvent) only for a minute period.

For large system sizes, \(N_{0}\) begins to increase at \(T>0.8\). This trend is also consistent with the overlap of plane wave solutions (crystal), since their boundaries to each other are somewhat reminiscent of the trajectories of a particle of heat (spin) in a spin glass. This thermal glass transition is possibly more of a priori than posterior [30]. Along with the phase transition, \(N_{0}\) transforms to reveal the presence of a genuine glass transition, which occurs when \(N_{0}>2\), beyond which the propagation of spin glass order parameter spurs the direction of the insulator state transition (for the model that includes competing forces) or the ballistic order state transition (for the model that does not have competing forces). There are three distinct phases before \(N_{0}\) vanishes and the system enters the glassy state. The initial phase, representing the linear ordering of degrees of freedom, can be regarded as an overfilling of the competition between the different orientation moments in an ice crystal, and the disordered to the ordered transition lies in the intermediate region. At temperatures once a macroscopic amount of magnetite has accumulated in the system, the weak next-nearest-neighbor frustration between the different directions of the magnetic moments causes a temporary phase separation, then differences between the magnetic moments gate the motion of the charges to thereby achieve an indefinite thermal glass transition. The three phases mentioned above can indeed be distinguished by considering the spectral properties of the Hamiltonian’s associated with the different configurations. Figures 9, 10 and 11 illustrate the physical nature of the phases of the aα spin glass and the phase transition, and the order of transition between them (from low to high temperature) based on the differences in the structure of the corresponding eigenspectrum. The non-zero spin glass order parameters in the vicinity of two entropic neighbors, in all relevant systems [Fig. 10(a)] including dipolar spin glass, non-net energy-spin-spin, and spin glass associated with competing forces (such as spin-ice vectors in spin glasses of dipolar interactions [12, 40].] or in zero energy pairs of mostly orthogonal spins [Fig. 10(c)], have the same statistical structure as the spins are distributed across long bars of the self-avoiding simple cubic lattice extending from \(x=-2\) to \(x=3\). At energies (energies-based) higher than the absolute value of the next-nearest-neighbor distance, the sign of the magnetization at t=0 distorts so much that to the eye a vortex arc is formed on the lattice after rescaling by the factor \(\exp(t/2D)\) with a cm~nm spacing (due to the typical separation of the nearest neighbors of 1.5D-d [12, 40] asymptotically and of 3D-d asymptotically [42, 44]; Fig. 10(b)). Likewise, in models of utilizing the Heisenberg Hamiltonian feature, depending on the system size, a net spin either is located in a Van der Waals dimer or a crystal lattice, which may be attributed to the local symmetry of the spin units in the disordered phase [Fig. 11].
